quotes.text:
I think this is what wyrd actually means, human worth that was never about being static, never about being plotted somewhere along someone else’s bell curve, but about always moving, always still taking shape.

Let’s embrace our wyrd, weirdness, and everyone else’s too.
quotes.source: Helen Edgar, Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal, More Realms, July 2026.

records.text: Specimen Monotropa uniflora L. — the ghost pipe, the Indian pipe, the ghost plant Named Carl Linnaeus, Species Plantarum, 1753. Monotropa, one turn, for the arched stem; uniflora, one-flowered Also mounted Emily Dickinson to Mabel Loomis Todd, 30 September 1882 (Letter 997), and Dickinson’s poem ‘Tis whiter than an Indian pipe, about 1879 (Fr1513A) Following Helen Edgar, Monotropa Uniflora and Monotropism, More Realms, 7 July 2026 — written for the fifth anniversary of Dinah Murray’s death, and the reason this sheet exists Read 9 September 2026 Read by Ryan Boren Biology Not here. The mechanism — myco-heterotrophy, carbon taken from fungi and none given back — is our sibling site’s: Star Stuff, A Field Guide to Symbioses. This sheet has the naming, the letter, the poem, and the word Terms Monotropism · Neuroqueer · Interdependence · Flow state There is a plant in the deep shade of North American, Latin American and East Asian forests that carries no green at all. It cannot photosynthesise. It does not reach for the light. It draws everything it needs from fungal threads in the soil, which draw theirs from the roots of trees — so the plant lives, entirely, on a connection nobody above ground can see. Linnaeus named it in 1753 for the single turn of its stem. Emily Dickinson pressed it into a herbarium, wrote a poem about it, and called it the preferred flower of life. Two hundred and thirty-eight years after the naming, an Autistic researcher and her neighbour reached for the same Greek root to describe a mind whose attention runs in one deep channel instead of many shallow ones.

records.heading: Seven hands on one specimen
records.text: This sheet is a wall rather than a reading, and the difference is not decoration. A reading has an order and an argument that arrives at the end. A wall has a chorus: many people, across two hundred and seventy years, standing in front of the same object and each seeing something the others could not. A herbarium sheet that has been in a cabinet long enough looks exactly like this — a specimen, and a stack of determination slips in different hands, every one of them signed.

quotes.text: That without suspecting it you should send me the preferred flower of life, seems almost supernatural, and the sweet glee that I felt at meeting it, I could confide to none.
quotes.source: Emily Dickinson to Mabel Loomis Todd, 30 September 1882 — Letter 997, in pencil. Todd had sent her a painted panel of Indian pipes six days earlier.

quotes.text:
This limitless Hyperbole
Each one of us shall be -
‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis
It be not Tragedy -
quotes.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘Tis whiter than an Indian pipe, about 1879 — the last quatrain, from R. W. Franklin’s reading of Amherst Manuscript 483 (Fr1513A).

quotes.text: He meant, perhaps, that the androgynous mind is resonant and porous; that it transmits emotion without impediment; that it is naturally creative, incandescent and undivided.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, chapter VI (Hogarth Press, 1929), pp. 148–149. The he is Coleridge, and Woolf is guessing at what he meant — twice, with a perhaps in each clause.

quotes.text: Attention without feeling, I began to learn, is only a report. An openness — an empathy — was necessary if the attention was to matter.
quotes.source: Mary Oliver, Our World (Beacon Press, 2007). Transcribed by Ryan Boren from his own copy. Not from Upstream, which is where this sentence is usually credited — see the label correction below.

quotes.text: I haven’t really ever had a career, I’ve had a mission.
quotes.source: Dinah Murray, interviewed by Kate Fox in Dalgety Bay about a month before her death on 7 July 2021, quoted in Fox’s tribute, 16 August 2021. Fox titled the poem she read at the memorial Monotropa Uniflora.

quotes.text: It is a plant that refuses to be binary at the root of its being, in the same way it refuses to draw its nourishment from sunlight, the way other plants are expected to.
quotes.source: Helen Edgar, Monotropa Uniflora and Monotropism, More Realms, July 2026. Monotropa uniflora is a perfect flower in the botanical sense — stamens and pistil in one bloom.

quotes.text: The quality of presence that the world persistently mistakes for absence, the inner life that runs deeper than it appears from the outside?
quotes.source: Helen Edgar, same essay, on what the it of Dickinson’s poem might be. Her sentence ends in a question mark and it is left here, because she is asking rather than concluding.

records.heading: One root, three turns
records.text: The Greek monotropos means turning one way. Linnaeus took it for the arched stem of a flower. Two centuries later two women in London took it for a mind. Nobody planned the rhyme, and it is not a metaphor either: it is the same word, describing the same shape twice. monotropos Greek Turning one way; of a single turn. Monos, one, and tropos, a turn — the same tropos that gives English trope, a turn of phrase. Monotropa 1753 Linnaeus’s genus, in Species Plantarum. The turn is physical: the stem arches over so the single flower hangs facing the ground. A plant named for the direction it bends. monotropism 1991 onward Attention pooled in one deep channel rather than spread thin across many. Coined by Dinah Murray with her neighbour Jeanette Buirski, and set out in Murray, Lesser and Lawson’s 2005 paper. A turn you are, not a turn you make. The 2005 paper is Murray, Lesser and Lawson, Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism, in Autism 9(2), 139–156. Its third author is Wenn Lawson, and the journal’s byline still reads Wendy Lawson. He is a trans man who has published under Wenn for years, and a citation that reproduces a publisher’s record over a living author’s own name is not neutral accuracy — it is a database outranking a person. We cite him as Wenn Lawson and say what the byline says, so a reader can find the paper and nobody has to be deadnamed to do it.

records.heading: Two hands, and one of them is the same hand
records.text: Mabel Loomis Todd painted a panel of Indian pipes and sent it to Emily Dickinson in September 1882. Dickinson wrote back within days, in pencil, and told her she had sent the preferred flower of life. Eight years later, when Todd and T. W. Higginson brought out the first posthumous Poems, that painting went on the cover. Todd is also one of the two editors who tidied Dickinson. Sheet No. 6 is about what they did to Wild nights: Higginson wrote let us alter as little as possible and then printed the poem with eight of its nine dashes gone. The hand that gave Dickinson her favourite flower is the hand that regularised her punctuation. That is not hypocrisy and it is not a scandal — it is what editing was, and Todd is the reason a great deal of Dickinson survived at all. It is simply worth saying that the same person can be the gift and the alteration, and that a reader who only has the tidied text cannot tell. Gift and alteration, one hand.

records.heading: A poem, and what 1896 did to it
records.text: Three years before the letter, Dickinson had already written the plant down. The poem survives on a fragment of stationery, in pencil, about 1879. She left herself alternatives, and the first editors took them. Franklin records three words Dickinson wrote in as options: denote for imply in line 5, designate for intimate in line 6, and What customs for What function in line 8. When the poem was first printed in Poems (1896) it appeared as three quatrains, with the alternatives for lines 5 and 8 adopted — so the version that circulated read denote and What customs, and the version above is the one on the paper. Neither reading is a mistake. She wrote both. But an editor choosing between a poet’s alternatives, silently, and printing the result as the poem is the same move as removing her dashes, and it is the move this collection keeps finding. The alternatives are the poem too. A text that has had its options resolved for you is a text with a decision hidden in it. ‘Tis Drama — if Hypothesis It be not Tragedy

quotes.text:
‘Tis whiter than an Indian Pipe -
‘Tis dimmer than a Lace -
No stature has it, like a Fog
When you approach the place -
Not any voice imply it here -
Or intimate it there -
A spirit - how doth it accost -
What function hath the Air?
This limitless Hyperbole
Each one of us shall be -
‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis
It be not Tragedy -
quotes.source: Emily Dickinson, about 1879. Amherst Manuscript 483, in pencil on a fragment of stationery. Text from R. W. Franklin, The Poems of Emily Dickinson: Variorum Edition (Belknap Press, 1998), Fr1513A, as published in the Emily Dickinson Archive.

records.heading: She kept a herbarium, which is what this site is
records.text: Dickinson assembled more than four hundred pressed plants as a young woman, mounted and labelled, and the album is now in Harvard’s Houghton Library — the same library that holds the manuscript on Sheet No. 6. Monotropa uniflora is in it. This site is drawn as a herbarium sheet because the form makes an attribution argument: a specimen is somebody else’s, a label is where we speak, and the line between them is drawn in the layout rather than left to a reader’s good faith. It is a slightly strange thing to discover that the poet on two of our sheets was doing the same thing at nineteen, with real plants, in an album, in Amherst. Which is also the answer to the question people keep asking about her life. From outside it looked like a withdrawal. From the letters, the poems, and four hundred labelled specimens, it looks like the opposite: attention pooled, at length, on a small number of things, with enormous care. There is a word for that now, and the word shares a root with the flower.

records.heading: Not a tragedy
records.text:
The plant is white because it has given up chlorophyll. It has no leaves. It grows in the dark, on the forest floor, out of leaf litter, and it feeds through fungi that feed through trees. By every measure a plant is usually judged by, it is failing at being a plant. It is also perfectly well. It is not a parasite on trees and not a saprophyte on rot, which is what botanists thought for a century; it is a myco-heterotroph, and the arrangement works. The plant is not doing without a connection to light. It is connected to light through somebody else. That is not a lesser way to be alive, and Star Stuff has the numbers on how the carbon actually moves. Dickinson’s last line does not say the thing is a tragedy. It says: ‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis / It be not Tragedy - — which reads, turned around, as a hope with a condition on it. Helen puts the same thought without the subjunctive: the ghost pipe is not a tragedy, and neither are Autistic people, and both thrive when the conditions are right rather than when they are corrected. What this sheet will not tidy We are not claiming Dickinson was Autistic, and neither is Helen — she says so in as many words on her own page. Monotropism is a theory of attention that many Autistic people recognise; a nineteenth-century poet cannot be assessed by resemblance, and reading her life through a word coined in 1991 is our doing, not hers. The rhyme between the plant and the theory is a coincidence of vocabulary, not evidence of anything. Linnaeus named a stem’s curve. Murray and Buirski named a pattern of attention. That both reached for monotropos is lovely and it proves nothing about either. This sheet has no plate. Every mounted image on this site is a public-domain botanical print or painting, and we do not have one of Monotropa uniflora. The Dickinson manuscript is available but licensed, the modern photographs are in copyright, and Todd’s painted panel — the object at the centre of the letter — we could not clear. If you know of a public-domain Monotropa uniflora plate, it belongs here. Say so and it will be. The plant blackens and collapses when handled, and Helen reads that as recognisable. We have kept her reading in her words rather than generalising it, because maybe it’s just me who relates in this way is in her sentence and taking it out would make a shared claim out of a personal one. The biology here is deliberately thin. Myco-heterotrophy is a mechanism with numbers attached and those belong to our sibling site, which risks a wrong fact where this one risks a wrong attribution. If you want to know how the carbon moves, go there. Dinah Murray spent her last years photographing lichens and mushrooms on the Fife coast — the same kingdom of organisms this plant lives through, attended to closely, for their own sake, by someone who had given the world a word for exactly that kind of attention. Kate Fox called the memorial poem Monotropa Uniflora. It was the right name. Provenance

Specimen On Being Ill Maker Virginia Woolf First printed The New Criterion, January 1926 This text The Hogarth Press, 1930 — revised by Woolf, and set in type by her Read 7 September 2026 Read by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren Woolf wrote the essay about illness that English did not have, complained inside it that English could not hold one, and then went back four years later and quietly made her own sentences stranger. This sheet mounts the text as she left it in 1930.

records.heading: Illness has no place in literature
records.text: The essay opens with a list of what a temperature does to a person — the undiscovered countries, the wastes and deserts of the soul, the ancient and obdurate oaks uprooted by a bout of flu — and then lands on a complaint about the shelf: Specimen — the missing theme Novels devoted to influenza, she says; epic poems to typhoid; odes to pneumonia, lyrics to tooth-ache. It is a joke and it is not a joke. Love and battle and jealousy are the themes that got the canon, and every one of them is something a body does while upright and in motion. The condition that stops the body is the one the shelf has no room for. This is a claim about literature, and it is also a claim about who gets to be a subject. A century of Disabled and chronically ill writers have made the second claim directly. Woolf makes the first, in 1926, and leaves the second sitting underneath it.

quotes.text: …it becomes strange indeed that illness has not taken its place with love and battle and jealousy among the prime themes of literature.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: The language runs dry
records.text: Her explanation for the gap is not squeamishness. It is vocabulary. Specimen — the poverty of the language It has all grown one way. A language is a record of what its speakers were required to be able to say. Hamlet got four centuries of vocabulary; the shiver got none. So the person in the bed is left, in Woolf's account, with nothing ready made — forced to coin words himself, and, taking his pain in one hand, and a lump of pure sound in the other… so to crush them together that a brand new word in the end drops out. She then does it herself. Chloral hydrate, the sedative she reaches for, arrives in the essay as that mighty Prince with the moths' eyes and the feathered feet, one of whose names is Chloral — a mythological figure invented on the spot because the pharmacological name will not carry what the drug means at four in the morning. Where we take this next is ours and not hers. Coining words for what the language has no room for is exactly what Autistic and Disabled communities have spent decades doing — monotropism, neuroqueer, bodymind, spoons. Woolf is describing one sufferer, one headache, and one doctor in the nineteen-twenties. She is not anticipating a lexicon that people would build a hundred years later out of their own lives. Reading her sentence forward to meet it is our move. The observation that the language grew one way is hers.

quotes.text: English, which can express the thoughts of Hamlet and the tragedy of Lear, has no words for the shiver and the headache. It has all grown one way.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: Deserters
records.text: Then comes the sentence this sheet is named for. Woolf has been describing the effort health demands — the genial pretence, the endless obligation to communicate and share and work together — and the moment it stops: Specimen — the army of the upright Normativity, named as a posture. Not a belief, not an attitude — a way of holding the body that the rest of it is conscripted into. The army of the upright. Vertical, mobile, productive, on time. An inch of foot above the floor is enough to break the enlistment. What makes the sentence hold is that Woolf does not treat desertion as defeat. The deserter is the one who can finally look round, to look up—to look, for example, at the sky. The upright never see it: their sky is mutilated by chimneys and churches and serves as a background for man. Lying down is what gives it back. An essay that had only complained about being ill would not be on this site. This one says the position everyone is arranged into is a position, and that leaving it lets you see.

quotes.text: Directly the bed is called for, or, sunk deep among pillows in one chair, we raise our feet even an inch above the ground on another, we cease to be soldiers in the army of the upright; we become deserters. They march to battle.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: The body intervenes
records.text: Underneath both arguments is a third, and it is the one that has aged least: Specimen — a sheet of plain glass The creature within, she writes, can only gaze through the pane — smudged or rosy — and cannot separate off from the body like the sheath of a knife or the pod of a pea for a single instant. That is a refusal of the mind–body split, written plainly, decades before the word bodymind was available to say it in one breath. Again: the word is not hers, and we are not putting it in her mouth. The refusal is.

quotes.text: …literature does its best to maintain that its concern is with the mind; that the body is a sheet of plain glass through which the soul looks straight and clear, and, save for one or two passions such as desire and greed, is null, and negligible and non-existent. On the contrary, the very opposite is true. All day, all night the body intervenes.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: What this sheet will not tidy
records.text: The same essay is snobbish about the people doing the caring, and it reaches for empire when it wants a figure for effort. Sympathy, Woolf writes, is dispensed chiefly by the laggards and failures, women for the most part… who, having dropped out of the race, have time to spend upon fantastic and unprofitable excursions. She then names three of them by their initials, with real affection — the friend who builds up the nursery fender by the sickroom fire, the one who would ransack London for a giant tortoise to solace you. They are the reason the essay exists. They are also, in her sentence, the ones who lost. And the labour of staying upright is to communicate, to civilise, to share, to cultivate the desert, educate the native, to work together by day and by night to sport. The desert and the native are doing figurative work in a list about going to the office. That is the imperial imagination supplying a metaphor without being asked, in 1926, in a sentence about being tired. Neither of these is a reason to put the essay down, and neither gets softened here. An essay can see the arrangement of the upright with total clarity from inside the bed and still not see the arrangement of the sickroom it is lying in — who is paid, who is unpaid, who is a woman, who dropped out of a race she was never going to be allowed to win. Woolf is describing care work as the occupation of people with nothing better to do, while being kept alive by it. The sharpest reading of normativity in the essay is the one it does not turn on itself.

records.heading: She revised her own sentence
records.text: One more thing, and it is the reason this sheet names its edition on the label. On Being Ill exists in two states Woolf authorised. It appeared in The New Criterion in January 1926, and she revised it for the Hogarth Press edition of 1930 — two hundred and fifty signed copies, the type set by her. The revisions are not corrections. In the first paragraph alone: The first paragraph, 1926 and 1930 1926, The New Criterion 1930, The Hogarth Press brings to light brings to view uprooted in us in the act of sickness uprooted in us by the act of sickness when we think of this and infinitely more when we think of this with love, battle, and jealousy with love and battle and jealousy is null, negligible and non-existent is null, and negligible and non-existent Look at the last two. In 1926 those are lists, punctuated the way a list is supposed to be punctuated. In 1930 the commas open out into and…and…and, and the sentences stop being tidy. Love and battle and jealousy arrive one after another with no rest between them. Null, and negligible and non-existent piles up instead of resolving. It is the same move the essay is about. A writer who has just argued that the language grew one way went back into her own prose and un-grew it a little — in the direction of the breath, and away from the rule. She did it four years later, in type she set with her own hands, on a page she owned outright because the press was hers. So the edition is not a footnote here. Quote the 1926 commas and you are quoting Woolf. Quote the 1930 and…and…and and you are also quoting Woolf. Quote one and date it to the other and you have made a claim about her that is not true. This sheet reads 1930 because the revision is part of what it is reading. The 1926 text is scanned and online, and it is worth putting beside this one.

records.heading: In their indifference
records.text:
The essay ends up among flowers, because the deserter, flat on her back, has time to look at them properly. Woolf watches the sky first and finds it divinely beautiful… also divinely heartless — immeasurable resources spent on something with nothing to do with human profit. Then she looks down at the rose, which has been standing still and steady in the earth all afternoon while nobody watched. Specimen — the comfort Not that the flowers care. That they do not, and are therefore not asking anything of you. Nothing in that garden requires you to be upright, on time, or getting better. It is the one relation in the essay with no demand in it — and Woolf finds it, characteristically, at the exact moment she has stopped being able to stand up. Provenance

quotes.text: It is in their indifference that they are comforting.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.text: This is the privacy policy, and it is short because there is little to describe. This site is a folder of files on a web host. It runs no analytics, sets no cookies, has no accounts, no comments, and no advertising, and it makes no requests to anybody else’s server. There is one field on the whole site, on the finding aid, and it never submits anywhere — see below. Two things nevertheless happen when you read a page, and both are below. Last updated 9 September 2026. Any change to this page gets an entry in the accession register, the same as a correction to a sheet — so we may update this policy from time to time is not something we have to ask you to accept on trust.

records.heading: What your own browser keeps
records.text: Two values, in your browser’s local storage, put there only if you press one of the two controls at the top of every page: qe-ground Which ground you asked for — the daylight sheet or the cabinet. Holds the word daylight or cabinet, and nothing else. qe-plain Whether you asked for plain view, which switches off the display faces, the wonk, the rotation and the motion. Holds 1, or is absent. Neither is a cookie and neither is ever sent anywhere. Local storage is not attached to requests the way a cookie is; these two values stay in the browser that wrote them, on the device that wrote them. We cannot read them, and nothing on this site tries to. Clearing your site data removes them and the page goes back to following your system’s own light or dark preference. They identify nobody. There is no visitor id here, random or otherwise, and no way to recognise a returning reader.

records.heading: What the host sees
records.text: The site is served by Netlify, which acts as our hosting processor. Asking any web server for a page necessarily tells it who is asking, so Netlify’s access logs record your IP address, your browser’s user-agent string, and which address you requested. Under the GDPR an IP address is personal data, which is why this page exists at all. We do not use those logs for analytics and we do not build anything from them. The lawful basis is legitimate interests — serving the site and keeping it up. We do not set or control their retention period, and we would rather say that plainly than name a number we cannot enforce; Netlify’s own privacy notice governs what it keeps and for how long.

records.heading: What is deliberately not here
records.text: No analytics of any kind. No page-view counter, no tag manager, no heatmap, no session recording. We do not know how many people read this. No cookies. The word document.cookie does not appear anywhere in this site’s code, which is why there is no consent banner: there is nothing to consent to, and a banner would be theatre. No third-party requests. Until 9 September 2026 the pages loaded their two typefaces from Google’s font CDN, which told Google your IP address and user agent on every page load, before you had read a word. The fonts are now served from this domain and that request is gone. It was the only one. No accounts and no comments, and nothing that submits. There is exactly one place on this site to type: the search field on the finding aid. It has no server behind it. What you type is matched against a file your browser has already downloaded, inside your browser, and it is never sent anywhere — not to us, because there is no us to send it to. Until 9 September 2026 this line said there was nowhere on the site to type anything at all; the field is new and the line was corrected in the same change that added it, which is in the register. No advertising, and nothing sold or shared. There is no commercial arrangement here to share anything under.

records.heading: What you search for
records.text: The finding aid searches this whole site, and it does the searching in your browser. Your browser fetches one file from this domain — search-index.json, the text of every page — and everything after that happens on your machine. There is no search server, no search API, and no third party involved, so the request our host logs is a request for that one file and nothing about what you were looking for. The search term is not in the address, and that is deliberate. The usual way to make a search shareable is ?q=, which is part of the URL a browser sends — so every term anybody typed would be written into the hosting log described above. Here it goes after the # instead: /search#q=lavender. Browsers never send the part after the # to a server. The link is still shareable and still bookmarkable, and the word you searched for reaches nobody, including us. Nothing about a search is remembered. There is no history of recent searches, nothing added to local storage, and the two values described at the top of this page are still the only two things this site stores. One thing worth being plain about, since it is the general case and not ours: your browser’s own address bar may remember the address, fragment and all. That is your browser’s history on your own device, not something this site does or can see — but on a shared machine it is the copy that would tell somebody what you looked up.

records.heading: Links to other places
records.text: Nearly every sheet cites its sources, so the pages are full of links out — to journals, archives, libraries, and the writers we are reading. Following one of those takes you somewhere we do not control, and that site will see you arrive under its own policy, not this one. The one thing we do about it: every response here sends Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, so a site you click through to is told that you came from queering.earth and is not told which page you were reading. Which sheet you had open is nobody else’s business.

records.heading: Your rights, and why most of them have nothing to work on
records.text: Under the UK and EU GDPR you have the right to access your personal data, to have it corrected or erased, to restrict or object to its processing, to portability, and to complain to a supervisory authority. Those rights are real and we are not qualifying them. But we hold no store of reader data for them to reach. There is no database, no mailing list, and no account. The only personal data connected to your reading of this site is in a hosting log we do not own, and we could not find your record in it if you asked, because we have nothing to match you against. If you want that log addressed, Netlify is the party who holds it. If you are in the UK you can complain to the Information Commissioner’s Office; elsewhere in Europe, to your own national authority.

records.heading: Who we are
records.text: Queering Earth is a collaboration between the Stimpunks Foundation and More Realms, who are the joint controllers for anything described above. For a privacy question, or for anything else about this site, either of those sites will reach us, and the repository’s issues are the fastest route — that is where corrections to the sheets are raised too, and they are answered in public. Not legal advice, and not written by a lawyer. This page describes what the code does, and it was checked against the code rather than adapted from a template. If it is wrong about a fact, that is a correction and it belongs in the register — say so and it will be.

Specimen Promises like Pie-crust Maker Christina Rossetti Written 20 April 1861 — the date her brother read off her notebooks First printed New Poems (Macmillan, 1896), edited by William Michael Rossetti — thirty-five years later, and two years after her death This text The 1896 first printing, pages 130–131. Line 20 keeps its colon Read 8 September 2026 Read by Ryan Boren Read alongside Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti (2026), Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity Terms Caves, campfires, watering holes · Shared-air space · Monotropism · Co-regulation In 1861 Christina Rossetti wrote twenty-four lines refusing to promise anybody anything, and put them in a notebook. A hundred and sixty-five years later a paper in Feminism & Psychology gave the thing she was refusing a name — the relationship escalator — and asked what would happen if Autistic people were told, early, that stepping off it was allowed. This sheet reads the poem as the permission slip nobody handed me. Specimen — the poem, entire

quotes.text:
Promise me no promises,
So will I not promise you:
Keep we both our liberties,
Never false and never true:
Let us hold the die uncast,
Free to come as free to go:
For I cannot know your past,
And of mine what can you know?

You, so warm, may once have been
Warmer towards another one:
I, so cold, may once have seen
Sunlight, once have felt the sun:
Who shall show us if it was
Thus indeed in time of old?
Fades the image from the glass,
And the fortune is not told.

If you promised, you might grieve
For lost liberty again:
If I promised, I believe
I should fret to break the chain:
Let us be the friends we were,
Nothing more but nothing less:
Many thrive on frugal fare
Who would perish of excess.
quotes.source: Christina Rossetti, Promises like Pie-crust, written 20 April 1861. Text from the first printing in New Poems by Christina Rossetti, Hitherto Unpublished or Uncollected, edited by William Michael Rossetti (New York and London: Macmillan, 1896), pages 130–131, read in two separate scanned copies of that edition. Public domain. The alternating indent is hers as printed; the spaces the compositor set before every colon are not, and are closed up here — see below.

records.heading: Promise me no promises
records.text: I read Promises like Pie-crust as liberation from eternal vows and possessive romance into something more compatible with my ways of being. Look at what the first stanza actually declines. Not the other person — the promise. Not the closeness, but the claim. Keep we both our liberties is a plural: the poem is not protecting one party from the other, it is protecting the same thing in both of them, and it treats that thing as the precondition for anything else. Then it goes further and declines certainty itself: Never false and never true. The die is held, uncast. Not thrown and lost, not put away — held, in the hand, with the outcome still open. Cisgender heterosexual monogamy has always been a bad fit for me. The poem helped me develop my solo polyamorous and pansexual identity.

records.heading: The escalator, and not knowing there was a way off
records.text: The thing Rossetti is standing beside without a name for it got named in 2026, in a paper built out of the words of forty-six Autistic adults. The authors borrow the term from Amy Gahran: the relationship escalator, the single moving staircase from dating to exclusivity to cohabitation to marriage to children to lifelong monogamy, on which every step both proves and demands the next. Specimen — the false assumption What the paper is really about is not the escalator. It is the cost of not being told there is a way off it. Specimen — the consequences of not knowing Which is where a poem comes in. A twenty-four-line refusal, printed in 1896 and sitting on the shelf ever since, is one of the few places a person could have found the idea before anybody thought to teach it.

quotes.text: There are a great many social normativities … and “social scripts” such as the relationship escalator, all of which are based around the false assumption that humans don’t vary.
quotes.source: Liriava, 53, genderqueer, pansexual, LGBTQ+ group, quoted in Monique Huysamen, Chris Hatton and Marianthi Kourti, Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity, Feminism & Psychology, 2026. The ellipsis is in the paper.

quotes.text: Together, these narratives reveal the consequences of not knowing – and not being supported to know – about possibilities for intimate relationships beyond cisgender heterosexual monogamy.
quotes.source: Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity, 2026.

records.heading: Free to come as free to go
records.text: The totalizing expectations of traditional romantic relationships are incompatible with me. They are excessive to the point of overwhelm and burnout. I need quiet parallel existence in a shared campfire setting and solo recharge time in a cave setting by myself. I need intermittent relationships where the die is held uncast, free to come as free to go. Shared-air space relationships of any sort are intensive pattern dances done at the terrifying tempo of synchronous, full-sensory real-time. I need daily doses of solitude and regular hibernation intervals to sustainably withstand any other human being. Only in solitude do I have the space to unfurl my patterns, un-beset by the outside, and recline into their regulated peace. Tab. V, Tecoma ceramensis, from Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi, volume 1 (Amsterdam: C. G. van der Post, 1863). Drawn by A. Bernecker, signed A. Bernecker. del. in the lower left; chromolithographed by Emrik & Binger of Haarlem, whose imprint is in the lower right. Public domain; scanned from the Missouri Botanical Garden, Peter H. Raven Library copy for the Biodiversity Heritage Library. I need my own rhythms and temporalities — and that phrase is the paper’s, describing exactly this: Specimen — counter-narratives Value independence rather than framing it as a deficit. That sentence is doing a lot of quiet work. The clinical literature has spent decades reading a preference for one’s own home, one’s own bed and one’s own schedule as social impairment. Here it is read as a relationship structure, which is what it is. Specimen — my own home environment

quotes.text: These narratives resist and queer the heteronormative, neuronormative, ableist expectations of ‘the relationship escalator’, complete dependence, coliving and cosleeping as the defining features of a legitimate relationship. They offer counter-narratives following their own rhythms and temporalities, and value independence rather than framing it as a deficit.
quotes.source: Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity, 2026.

quotes.text: I tried sharing a home with a partner in the past, and it did not work for me. I prefer being in control of my own home environment and having a flexible schedule. I also prefer being by myself when I am not feeling well, particularly when I am not feeling well mentally.
quotes.source: PhotonPulse_he_him, 47, male, heterosexual, men’s group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

records.heading: Many thrive on frugal fare
records.text: Every line speaks to me, especially the ending: Specimen — the last two lines Read that as a sensory statement and it stops being a proverb about modesty. Perish of excess is what happens to a body given more input than it can process — more contact, more noise, more presence, more obligation to be available. Rossetti reaches for frugal and excess, words about quantity, and puts thrive and perish on either side of them. Not better and worse. Different amounts, and a different amount is fatal. Tab. IV, Gonystylus miquelianus, from Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi, volume 1 (Amsterdam: C. G. van der Post, 1863). Signed van Aken et Bernecker, ad viv. del. — two hands, drawing from the living plant; chromolithographed by Emrik & Binger of Haarlem. Public domain; scanned from the Missouri Botanical Garden, Peter H. Raven Library copy for the Biodiversity Heritage Library. Mounted here for the weight of the thing, not as an argument. This is the same move Woolf makes on the first sheet on this plate: a claim that reads as temperament turns out, on inspection, to be a claim about a body.

quotes.text:
Many thrive on frugal fare
Who would perish of excess.
quotes.source: Rossetti, Promises like Pie-crust, 1861.

records.heading: Keep we both our liberties
records.text: I need time to immerse myself in my monotropic interests. My interests are a relationship in themselves. I immerse myself in them and get into flow states that are necessary to maintain regulation and mental health. Keep we both our liberties so that I may pursue my passions. Let us co-regulate together, and let us regulate apart pursuing our passions. Darwin drew the thing itself, without meaning to. A tendril of white bryony, caught on a twig at one end and held by its own stem at the other, contracts into a spiral — and the spiral runs one way from one end and the other way from the other, with a short straight stretch in the middle where the two turns meet. He printed it as Fig. 13 of The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants, captioned A caught tendril of Bryonia dioica, spirally contracted in reversed directions, and it is worth going to look at. One attachment, holding. Two ends, each turning its own way. The straight bit in the middle is where neither one gave in. Darwin is explaining a mechanical necessity — a tendril fixed at both ends cannot coil in a single direction without unwinding itself — and reading it as a diagram of anything else is entirely our doing. But it is the best picture of keep we both our liberties that anybody has drawn, and its author thought he was describing a weed. Specimen — there are concepts for this The definition of the second of those that I keep coming back to is Amanda Van Slyke’s, and it turns on ownership rather than on logistics: Specimen — solo polyamory No one owns one another. Rossetti gets there in the negative, a hundred and sixty years earlier, by declining to hand over the deed.

quotes.text: There are concepts such as Living Apart Together and solo polyamory which address the idea that relationships must include cosleeping and cohabitation.
quotes.source: Liriava, 53, genderqueer, pansexual, LGBTQ+ group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

quotes.text: Solo polyamory is the idea that people are autonomous beings who have different needs and wants, and alongside good communication and mutual respect between all partners, no one puts rules on each other because no one owns one another.
quotes.source: Amanda Van Slyke, How Polyamory Helped Me Advocate For My Needs As A Disabled Person, Thought.is.

records.heading: Not alone in needing to be alone
records.text: I’m not alone in my need to be, sometimes, alone. I’m not alone in my need for multiple different people with different ways of being to fill my life when it needs filling, to co-regulate me when I need to be with someone in a meaningful way to help balance and recharge the sensory system and bodymind. Plate 85 from Mordecai Cubitt Cooke, Illustrations of British Fungi (Hymenomycetes), volume 1 (London: Williams and Norgate, 1881–91). Two species on one plate: A is Agaricus (Lepiota) sistratus, in Gardens; B is Agaricus (Lepiota) mesomorphus, in woods. New Forest. Signed M.C.C. in the lower-left corner — Cooke’s own initials; his preface says the contributors’ initials are attached to their drawings. Public domain; scanned from the University of Toronto copy for the Biodiversity Heritage Library. One plate, two species, and not one specimen on it touching another. Every one at its own size, its own angle, its own stage of opening, on its own tuft of earth — one group found in gardens, the other in the New Forest, and arranged together on one sheet anyway. The paper’s participants over fifty say the not-knowing out loud, and it is the hardest part of it to read. Specimen — the nearest easiest offers Specimen — never taught this was an option Specimen — more than one way of doing it Three people, three decades apart, saying the same sentence: nobody told me. Not I chose wrong. I did not know there was a choice.

quotes.text: At the ripe age of 67, I can honestly say I wished I had followed less conventional relationships. With two failed heterosexual marriages (three kids all following pretty straight stuff) and a non-live-in 7 year partnership I feel like I missed out on aspects of love and intimacy just by responding to the nearest easiest offers.
quotes.source: Indigo_Regent_She_Her, 67, female, pansexual, mixed group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

quotes.text: I often think that if I had known polyamory was a thing when I was younger I would have chosen to form relationships in this way, but I was never taught this was an option or how to navigate these types of relationships.
quotes.source: MerryFennel, 39, female, bisexual, women’s group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

quotes.text: I struggled in my early 20s when I first tried to date in a neurotypical way and follow conventions, I did not know that there was more than one way of doing it.
quotes.source: NeuroGator, 50, nonbinary, lesbian, LGBTQ+ group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

records.heading: Let us neuroqueer relationships
records.text: Let us neuroqueer relationships so that they suit our authentic ways of being instead of forcing us to live in falsity. Tab. IX, Wormia subsessilis Miq., from Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi, volume 1 (Amsterdam: C. G. van der Post, 1863). Signed Th. Rocke, del. in the lower left; chromolithographed by Emrik & Binger of Haarlem. Public domain; scanned from the Missouri Botanical Garden, Peter H. Raven Library copy for the Biodiversity Heritage Library. Look at the leaves on that one plant. Green, russet, and a pale underside — painted as three different things because at the moment somebody sat down in front of it, they were three different things. A plate that averaged them into one correct leaf would be a worse record of the plant. That is close to where the paper lands, and the paper lands there as a demand on services rather than as a hope: Specimen — a neuroqueer ethic Specimen — on their own terms Specimen — shifting the course One thing worth saying about how that evidence was gathered, because the method is the argument too. The five focus groups were asynchronous and text-based, run on a forum over six weeks by an Autistic researcher, with participants anonymous to each other and free to arrive, leave and return at their own pace. The authors chose it deliberately, to make space for alternative temporalities. A study about people who need their own rhythms was built to run on them. Nobody had to sit in a circle and take turns at somebody else’s tempo in order to say that sitting in a circle at somebody else’s tempo does not work for them.

records.heading: A colon, where everyone else prints a full stop
records.text: Now the reason this sheet names its printing on the label. In the 1896 first printing, the poem’s lines end in colons. Eight of the twenty-four do, and there are exactly two full stops in the whole poem — at line 16, closing the second stanza, and at line 24, closing the poem. The text in general circulation, including the copy at the Poetry Archive, has three. The extra one lands here: Line 20, as printed 1896, New Poems, page 131 The text now in circulation I should fret to break the chain : I should fret to break the chain. A full stop there closes If you promised, you might grieve … I should fret to break the chain. into a finished sentence, and makes Let us be the friends we were a fresh proposal that follows it. The colon does something else: it makes the whole stanza one movement, in which the friendship is not a new offer but the consequence of everything said before the mark. Because a promise would cost you your liberty and cost me my peace — so let us be the friends we were. And the line that acquired the extra full stop is the line about breaking the chain. The colon is not one library’s smudge. It was read twice, in two separately scanned copies of the 1896 edition — the Princeton one and Victoria University’s in Toronto — and the mark, the alternating indent and the date line all agree. The Princeton pages were rendered as images and read rather than trusted to a text extractor, because a finding about one punctuation mark is not something an extractor is evidence about. Two things this sheet is not claiming. It is not claiming Rossetti’s manuscript, which we have not seen. Her brother printed from the seventeen notebooks she left, and he vouches in his preface for the accuracy of the dates in them; he says nothing about her punctuation, and he left no note on this poem at all. The colon is the earliest reading we can actually put our eyes on, not a certified one. Nor is it claiming that somebody deliberately changed the mark: a full stop in place of a colon at the end of a quatrain is the most ordinary silent tidying there is, and it may have happened in a schoolbook in 1930 and been copied ever since. What it claims is narrower and it holds: the earliest printing has a colon, the copies you will find have a full stop, and a sheet that quotes one while dating it to the other has said something untrue. The Woolf sheet is here for the same reason, in reverse — there the tidy commas turned out to be the author’s own earlier version, and the untidy and…and…and her later one. The lesson is not trust the older text. It is: name the printing, or do not quote. Two smaller things about the 1896 page, so that a reader who goes and looks is not confused. The first word of the poem is set as PROMISE after a large drop-cap P, which is how the volume opens every poem; the word is Promise. And the compositor set a space before every colon, semicolon and question mark, all through the book — that is the house style of the volume, not Rossetti’s pointing, so the spaces are closed up above. The title over the poem is in full capitals, again for every poem; the volume’s own contents page gives it as Promises like Pie-crust, which is the form this sheet uses. Modern editions mostly print it Promises Like Pie-Crust.

records.heading: What this sheet will not tidy
records.text:
Rossetti was not writing this. She wrote twenty-four lines in April 1861 to a you the printing does not name, and her brother, who dated the poem and published it, left no note saying who or why. She had no relationship escalator to step off, no word for what I am, and no reason on earth to be proposing an arrangement. Reading her refusal forward until it arrives at solo polyamory is our move, and it is the whole method of this site rather than a discovery about her. The language is hers. The use is mine. And the poem’s own bargain is not the one I am describing. Let us be the friends we were, nothing more but nothing less keeps the liberty by giving up the intimacy. What I want, and what the paper’s participants want, is the opposite trade: keep the intimacy, several of them, and give up the ownership. Rossetti hands back the whole thing. I am borrowing her terms for a deal she did not offer. The title is borrowed too, and we cannot say from whom. Promises and pie-crust are made to be broken was already proverbial when she used it. The attribution in circulation runs to Jonathan Swift’s Polite Conversation of 1738, which we have not read in a primary, and there are recorded uses earlier still. So this sheet names no owner for the saying rather than repeating one it has not checked. And Darwin’s tendril has a second half to it that the sheet has so far left out. Darwin says, on the same page, that the reversed spiral never occurs with uncaught tendrils; and when this appears to have occurred, it will be found that the tendril had originally seized some object and had afterwards been torn free. A coil is evidence of a hold. A coil on something holding nothing is evidence of a hold that ended. Nothing in the poem, and nothing on this sheet, makes that costless — a life of coming and going leaves a shape behind either way, and free to go and torn free are not the same event described twice. Independence is not automatically a happy ending, and the paper does not pretend it is. Set against every quotation above, from the same study, is this one: Specimen — growing old alone The authors do not resolve that, and neither will this sheet. Vero is not failing to want independence. She wants it, has it, needs paid support to have it, and is frightened by what it may cost her in forty years — because the people around her are still on the escalator, and a life off it is much lonelier than it needs to be when almost nobody else has been told they were allowed to step off. The scarcity is the problem, not the preference. That is an argument for more people knowing sooner, which is exactly what the paper asks for, and it is the argument a poem from 1861 has been quietly making from the shelf the whole time. Let us hold the die uncast. Provenance

records.text: Specimen William Shakespeare, The Tempest Maker William Shakespeare (1564–1616) First performed 1611. First printed in the First Folio, 1623 This text The play, the editorial history of one speech in it, and John William Waterhouse’s 1916 canvas, read together. The quotations are the play’s and the editors’; the sentences around them are ours, and this label is where we say so. Read 8 September 2026 Read by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren Terms Neuronormativity · Masking · Normal · Shared-air space Shakespeare, 1611 a boy actor, 1611 Theobald, 1733 Waterhouse, 1916 Huxley, 1932 Helen & Ryan, 2026 John William Waterhouse (1849–1917). Miranda – The Tempest, 1916, oil on canvas. Painted the year before Waterhouse’s death, forty-one years after his first, gentler Miranda of 1875. Public domain. Her face is turned away from us. One hand is pressed to her heart. Behind her a ship is coming apart on the rocks in cold, storm-grey light, and Waterhouse gives us none of Miranda’s expression to tell us how to feel about it, only the shape of a body absorbing someone else’s disaster as though it were happening inside her own chest. It is, art historians agree, the most emotionally exposed of his two attempts at her (DailyArt Magazine, n.d.). It is also, we want to argue, exactly the pose the play keeps putting her in: turned from us, feeling everything, granted almost none of the words that would let her account for what she feels. Miranda’s name is Shakespeare’s own coinage, the first recorded use of it as a person’s name in English (Wikipedia contributors, n.d.). He built it from the Latin gerundive of mirari, to wonder at: miranda, she who is to be wondered at, worthy of admiration. It is a lovely name and a loaded one, because wonder runs both ways. To wonder at something can mean to marvel at it with your whole, undivided attention. It can also mean to make of a person a spectacle: something looked at, remarked upon, held up as a curiosity, never quite the one doing the looking. This reading takes Shakespeare’s word and turns one preposition: not wondered at, which the play already does to her constantly, but wondered with, the way she herself wonders with the drowning sailors before anyone tells her to. We follow Miranda through all three, because the play cannot decide between them either, and because that argument, staged on one small island four hundred years before anyone invented the statistically normal person, is still the argument this whole project keeps having.

records.heading: Assembled, not born
records.text: Before any of that, one fact underneath the whole play. When The Tempest was first staged in 1611, Miranda would not have been played by a woman. English theatre would not permit that for another fifty years. She would have been played by a boy player, part of a company apprenticeship system in which performers of female roles were, on the surviving evidence, teenagers rather than children, commonly in their mid-to-late teens, cast for frame and voice and drilled in the gait, gesture, and vocal register that stood in for femininity on that stage (Kathman, 2005). Her modesty, her wonder, her compliant softness: every trait the play offers as Miranda’s nature was, at the moment of its first performance, a rehearsed construction laid onto a body the role needed nobody in the audience to think twice about. This is not a trivia footnote. It is Judith Butler’s argument about gender arriving three hundred and eighty years early and without ever citing Shakespeare: identity is not an interior truth that gesture and costume merely express, but a stylized repetition of acts, a performative accomplishment that both the audience and the performer come to believe in the doing of it (Butler, 1990). There was never a natural woman underneath Miranda for the boy actor to reveal. There was only the performance, repeated eight times a week until it read as nature. Waterhouse restages her in oil in 1916. This sheet restages her again in 2026. Nobody in this whole four-hundred-year chain ever got to meet an un-staged Miranda, including, arguably, Miranda.

records.heading: A household of three
records.text: Prospero was put to sea with his daughter when she was three years old, and for twelve years afterward their whole society is an island the size of a single household: a father, a daughter, and Caliban, with Ariel felt everywhere and seen by no one but Prospero. Miranda grows up with almost no comparison class. She has never seen a woman other than her own reflection, by her own account, and no man but her father, until Ferdinand. In the vocabulary Stimpunks’ own glossary uses, this is a shared-air space (Stimpunks Foundation, n.d.): physical, co-located presence, three bodies breathing the same weather for twelve years, rather than the digitally networked togetherness the term was coined to stand alongside. Twelve years on an island with three people is the household Miranda knows, and it is the only one she has ever had the chance to learn. None of this should read as an argument that isolation was secretly a gift. Alison Kafer’s work on crip time is useful precisely because it refuses to romanticise a slower or smaller world on principle, and instead keeps asking who gets to set its pace and shape (Kafer, 2013). Miranda did not choose the island and could not have left it. Prospero controlled the only boat, the only magic, and, for twelve years, the only company. Describing her household is not the same as approving of it, and the play never actually lets her answer that question on her own terms. The play, and four centuries of criticism after it, mostly cannot see this as anything but a wound waiting to be corrected by re-entry into the wider world. That correction has a name by the end of Act 5. We want to sit with the household of three a little longer before the crowd arrives.

records.heading: O, I have suffered with those that I saw suffer
records.text: The very first thing Miranda does on stage, before Prospero has told her anything, before she knows the wrecked men are staged, before she knows her own history, is feel the shipwreck in her body as though it were happening to her. Specimen — Act 1, Scene 2 She has not been asked to imagine their suffering. She has not calculated, from social cues, that suffering is the appropriate response. She simply reports it as a fact about her own body: I have suffered with those that I saw suffer. It is a strange verb tense for a play that has not shown her the wreck happening more than a moment before, and it reads less like sympathy performed for an audience than like attunement that runs ahead of explanation, feeling arriving before the story that would justify it. Waterhouse’s canvas, four hundred years later, paints exactly this line and nothing else: not Miranda deciding to care, but Miranda already, wordlessly, mid-suffering.

quotes.text:
If by your art, my dearest father, you have
Put the wild waters in this roar, allay them.
… O, I have suffered
With those that I saw suffer: a brave vessel,
Who had, no doubt, some noble creature in her,
Dash’d all to pieces.
quotes.source: The Tempest, Act 1, Scene 2 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

records.heading: Be collected. No more amazement.
records.text: And then, within a dozen lines, her father tells her to stop. Specimen — Act 1, Scene 2 This is not comfort so much as instruction. Prospero does not ask what she feels; he specifies what she is now permitted to feel, and issues it as a command in the imperative mood, before he has explained a single thing that would actually justify the reassurance. It is the same regulatory gesture the masque scene will later perform on her body, staged here first on her interior state: an outside authority deciding the correct amount and duration of someone else’s feeling. Reading this as an autistic reader might recognise it immediately, because it is the shape of every you’re fine delivered to a person who is, from the inside, plainly not being asked what fine would mean to them. Neuronormativity does not only police what a body does. It polices what a body is allowed to still be feeling once the socially appropriate window for feeling it has closed.

quotes.text:
Be collected.
No more amazement. Tell your piteous heart
There’s no harm done.
quotes.source: The Tempest, Act 1, Scene 2 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

records.heading: Abhorred slave
records.text: A few dozen lines later Miranda is given, in the First Folio of 1623, the hardest speech in the scene. Here is what four centuries of editing did to it. Miranda, First Folio, 1623 Reassigned to Prospero by editor Lewis Theobald, 1733, restored to Miranda in the Folger edition and others since (Folger Shakespeare Library, n.d.; Shakespeare Navigators, n.d.). It is a speech of real authority: an accusation, a claim to have been Caliban’s teacher, a judgment about who deserves what. Theobald moved it to Prospero’s mouth on the reasoning that it did not seem credible that a girl, taught language herself as a small child on the island, could plausibly have been the one who taught Caliban to speak (Shakespeare Navigators, n.d.). Many editions followed him for the better part of three centuries. The strikethrough above is not decoration. It is the actual editorial history: a name crossed out and a different name written over it, silently, in edition after edition, until it needed a restoration to notice it had happened at all. Notice what that eighteenth-century edit actually does. It is not a correction of a printing error; it is a decision about which register of speech a young woman is allowed to hold. Compassion, wonder, suffering-with: those stay hers without dispute. Judgment, command, the claim to have been someone’s teacher and to be entitled to be angry about the return on that labour: those get quietly reassigned to her father, because an editor two hundred years ago found her difficulty, her spikiness, less credible coming from her than from him. It is the same reflex this collection has already traced at the level of a whole language, the nineteenth-century invention of the statistically normal person against which everyone else became a deviation (Edgar, 2026). Here it happens a century earlier, at the level of a single attribution line in a single scene: whose hardness gets to be plausible, and whose has to be softened into someone else’s. It is also not an isolated case. Ann Thompson’s survey of Shakespeare’s editorial history finds the same reflex recurring across the canon, editors softening, reglossing, or reassigning a woman character’s harder or more sexually frank lines whenever those lines strained what the editor thought she should plausibly say. Adriana’s self-accusation in The Comedy of Errors has been glossed by more than one editor as her belatedly admitting a fault she never actually confesses to. The Quarto Othello’s more physically frank Desdemona was set aside by editors reaching for the Folio’s softer wording instead (Thompson, 2001). Theobald moving Miranda’s hardest speech into her father’s mouth is not one eccentric decision. It is a single instance of a pattern with a three-hundred-year paper trail, editors deciding, play after play, which register of speech a woman is allowed to be caught using.

quotes.text:
Abhorred slave,
Which any print of goodness wilt not take,
Being capable of all ill! I pitied thee,
Took pains to make thee speak, taught thee each hour
One thing or other…

records.heading: Before all sanctimonious ceremonies
records.text: Miranda’s courtship is not something that happens to her so much as something staged around her. Prospero engineers the shipwreck, times Ferdinand’s arrival, watches the two of them fall in love from a distance he has arranged, and later, at the betrothal masque, delivers a warning to his future son-in-law about his daughter’s body that Miranda is not recorded as hearing: Specimen — Act 4, Scene 1 This is heteronormativity staged as literal stagecraft: a father choreographing, timing, and finally verbally contracting his daughter’s marriage and its sexual terms, with magic standing in for all the ordinary social machinery that does the same work off an island. Caliban’s own line about Miranda, spoken earlier in the same scene of the play, makes plain what the stakes of that policing actually were: Specimen — Act 1, Scene 2 Miranda’s safety, in other words, was never secured by her own consent. It was secured by Prospero’s control of Caliban’s body, just as her marriage is secured by Prospero’s control of the entire scene Ferdinand walks into. Postcolonial readings of the play have long noted that Miranda’s own kindness toward Caliban, teaching him language, trying to civilise rather than simply subjugate him, is not an escape from her father’s colonial logic but a softer version of it: the missionary rather than the whip, aimed at the same outcome (see, broadly, the postcolonial critical tradition summarised in Lie, n.d.). We do not want to resolve that into either condemnation or credit. We want to leave it exactly as uncomfortable as it is: gentleness is not automatically outside empire’s reach.

quotes.text:
If thou dost break her virgin-knot before
All sanctimonious ceremonies may
With full and holy rite be minister’d…
quotes.source: The Tempest, Act 4, Scene 1 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

quotes.text:
O ho, O ho! would’t had been done!
Thou didst prevent me; I had peopled else
This isle with Calibans.
quotes.source: The Tempest, Act 1, Scene 2 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

records.heading: I’ll die your maid
records.text: And yet inside all that staging, Miranda does something the plot did not strictly require of her. She proposes. Specimen — Act 3, Scene 1 Read this against the boy actor and Butler’s stylized repetition of acts, and the moment gets sharper. Normative courtship in Miranda’s period had its own choreography of delay, indirection, and coyness, a script she has had no occasion to rehearse, because the only society available to rehearse it in was a household of three. What the scene reads as her innocence may be better read as a failure to perform the expected femininity correctly, and a failure that, instead of shaming her, becomes its own kind of honesty. She asks first. She names the terms herself. This is not a woman gracefully declining to know the rules. It is a directness the normative script has no room for, arriving anyway because nobody successfully installed the script in the first place. The scholar Jessica Slights has made a related case against reading Miranda as simply obedient and pliant, arguing that a girl raised entirely outside conventional courtship norms has no particular reason to have absorbed them, and that her willingness to ask first reads as a kind of independence her upbringing made possible rather than prevented (Slights, 2001). Both readings can be true at once. A person can be staged within someone else’s normativity and still, inside that staging, refuse to perform it correctly.

quotes.text:
I am your wife, if you will marry me;
If not, I’ll die your maid: to be your fellow
You may deny me; but I’ll be your servant,
Whether you will or no.
quotes.source: The Tempest, Act 3, Scene 1 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

records.heading: O, brave new world
records.text:
By Act 5, Miranda has spent twelve years in a household of three. Then Prospero’s magic delivers a dozen strangers onto the same small stage, and she says the line the whole play has been saving for her: Specimen — Act 5, Scene 1 Prospero’s reply is four words long and does not share her wonder: ’Tis new to thee. He knows, and the audience knows, that the goodly creatures in front of her include the brother who usurped him and the men who set them both adrift. The wider world being sold to Miranda as liberation is not new or brave at all; it is the same court politics that exiled her in the first place, now standing on her island in wet clothes. Sara Ahmed’s account of orientation is useful here: a body raised inside one small, particular arrangement of the world is not neutral before a bigger one, it has already been shaped by what it was given to reach toward, and a new world can bring a body up short exactly where that body was never built to fit (Ahmed, 2006). Miranda’s wonder is the sound of that arrival. It is not evidence that the wider world was actually the better one. Three centuries later Aldous Huxley took Miranda’s line, unedited and entirely straight-faced, as the title for a novel about a civilisation engineered for frictionless normality, and gave the same words, with the same devastating irony, to his own outsider character on first meeting that world (Huxley, 1932). The line has been doing this exact work for four hundred years: naming the gap between the crowded, normal world normativity promises and the narrower, stranger, more honestly peopled world it is actually asking you to trade away. Nothing in the text tells us whether Miranda’s household of three was worth less than the brave new world she is about to enter. It only tells us that nobody thought to ask her which she would have chosen. Nobody asked before the shipwreck. Nobody asked before the masque. Nobody asked before Theobald moved her hardest speech into her father’s mouth. Wonder, in the end, is the one register the play always lets her keep. It is worth noticing how much of everything else got quietly kept from her instead. What this reading will not tidy The Folio attribution of Abhorred slave to Miranda is the choice this sheet leans on, but it is a live editorial crux, not a settled fact; readers should hold the Theobald tradition in view rather than treat the Folio as simply correct. Reading Miranda’s education of Caliban as a softer colonialism is a critique of her kindness, not a defence of Prospero’s cruelty by comparison. Neither is offered here as the more forgivable option. Wonder is not evidence of freedom. A person can be genuinely delighted by a new world and still have had no say in whether they were delivered into it. We are the latest people to stage her. Nothing here is a neutral account of what the play really means; it is Helen and Ryan doing, deliberately and on the record, the thing the chain below has always been doing. This reading is built from a canonical, largely English, largely male lineage: Shakespeare, an Eton-educated novelist, a Royal Academy painter, and now two more writers. Neuroqueer theory’s own roots lie mostly outside that lineage, in mad studies and disability justice traditions that owe it little. Naming that we are one more link in this particular chain is not the same as having answered why this chain, rather than another, is the one worth extending. Restaged by Shakespeare, 1611 a boy actor, 1611 Theobald, 1733 Waterhouse, 1916 Huxley, 1932 Helen & Ryan, 2026 you, reading this Every entry in that chain believed it was the one finally looking at Miranda clearly. This is not an exemption from that pattern. It is a piece of neuroqueering, done on purpose, by two named people, in the sense Nick Walker gives the word: not a property the play or its heroine possesses, but a practice we are choosing to perform on it (Walker, 2021).
